title: The verb that must sit in second place
goal: Master the one rule that governs all Swedish word order — and the one English speakers break most often throughout their first year.
bekal: put a time expression at the front of a sentence without breaking its order
the second-place rule: whatever comes first, the verb is always number two
name the days of the week and the parts of the day

dialogs.title: Dialogue — På väg till tunnelbanan
dialogs.intro: Monday morning. Dian runs into Elin at the front door of the student housing; they're both heading for the same subway station.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: God morgon! Vart ska du idag?
lines.id: Good morning! Where are you off to today?
lines.literal: good morning! where-to shall you today?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Idag går jag till universitetet. Jag har en lektion klockan nio.
lines.id: Today I'm going to the university. I have a class at nine.
lines.literal: today go I to university-the. I have a lesson clock-the nine.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Då tar vi samma tåg. Jag jobbar på ett bibliotek i stan.
lines.id: Then we're taking the same train. I work at a library in town.
lines.literal: then take we same train. I work at a library in town-the.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: På morgonen är tunnelbanan alltid full.
lines.id: In the morning the subway is always packed.
lines.literal: in morning-the is subway-the always full.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Ja, men efter nio blir det bättre.
lines.id: Yes, but after nine it gets better.
lines.literal: yes, but after nine becomes it better.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.id: What are you doing this evening?

lines.speaker: Elin:

lines.text: På fredag är jag ledig. Ska vi fika då?
lines.id: I'm free on Friday. Shall we have a fika then?

lines.id: I'd love to! See you on Friday.

lines.id: Perfect. I'm running now — the train's coming!

notes: **Idag går jag** — not *idag jag går*. This one sentence teaches the whole unit. As soon as something else stands at the front of the sentence, the subject jumps behind the verb. If you say *idag jag går* ("today I go", perfectly normal English), Swedes will still understand you, but their ear trips over it — just as your ear would trip over "tomorrow I go will".

**Vart ska du?** is literally "where-to shall you?". The verb *gå* can be left out after *ska* when a direction is clear: *Vart ska du?* is a complete sentence on its own. Compare *Var är du?* — "where are you?", with no direction.

**Att gå** means **to walk**, not just "to go". If you travel by vehicle, the verb is **att åka**: *jag åker buss* (I go by bus), *jag åker tåg* (I go by train), *jag åker till Göteborg*. Saying *jag går till Göteborg* means you're really walking 470 kilometers.

**På morgonen, på kvällen** — parts of the day take *på* and the definite form (*morgonen*, not *morgon*): literally "in the morning", much as in English. Just learn these as set phrases; the *-en* ending stuck to the end of the noun is explained in the next unit.

**Sedan** (pronounced **SEN**, and often written just *sen* in casual writing) means "then, after that". It's one of the most common linking words in spoken Swedish, along with *och sen* — "and then".
**Gärna** has no single English equivalent. It means "gladly, I'd love to", and it's a one-word answer that is polite and warm at the same time. *Vill du ha kaffe?* — *Gärna!* Pronounced **YEH-nah**.

grammars.title: The verb-second rule (V2)
body: In a Swedish statement, **the verb is always the second element**. Not the second word — the second element. One element can be several words long (*på fredagsmorgonen*, *min bror och jag*), but it still counts as one.
What changes is not the verb but who stands in first place:
after: Look at the second column: **går, går, går, dricker, lagar** — it never moves. What moves is the subject, which gets pushed to third place every time something else comes first.

Why put something else first at all? Because that's where the **emphasis** goes. *Idag går jag till universitetet* stresses today (not tomorrow); *Jag går till universitetet idag* is a plain piece of information. Swedes front words as often as English speakers begin with "Today,…" or "On Friday,…" — the only difference is that Swedish then swaps the verb and subject. English still has a few fossils of this rule: "Here comes the bus", "There goes my train".
The rule also explains the question form you learned in Unit 2: in a yes/no question, first place is deliberately **left empty**, so the verb moves up to the front.

grammars.title: Days, and parts of the day
after: Days of the week are **not capitalized** in Swedish, and the final *-g* is almost always silent: *fredag* comes out as **FREH-dah**. Many of the names will look familiar — *tisdag, onsdag, torsdag, fredag* come from the same Norse gods as Tuesday to Friday.
"On Friday" is *på fredag*. If you mean "every Friday" or "on Fridays", it's plural: *på fredagar*. Just one letter's difference — but it separates a one-off plan from a weekly habit.

sections.title: The five most common word-order mistakes

blocks.text: They all have one cause: carrying English word order over word for word. English keeps subject-before-verb no matter what comes first; Swedish doesn't. Read the right-hand column aloud until it sounds natural.

head: Wrong
Right
Why
rows: something stands in front → the subject moves behind the verb
the question word takes place 1, the verb stays in place 2
*sedan* is an element too — it fills place 1

blocks.text: One check that always works: **count to two**. The first element can be anything, and as long as you like; the second must be the verb. If the second turns out to be *jag*, *vi* or *han*, the order is wrong.

blocks.title: Spaced review — back to Unit 1
items: Cover the Swedish column of the Unit 1 vocabulary, look at the English column, and say the Swedish words out loud.
Then rebuild these five sentences without looking: "My name is…", "I come from Indonesia", "Where do you live?", "Nice to meet you", "See you!".
Finally, say three of them with a time expression in front — *Idag är jag…*, *Ikväll bor jag…* — and feel the subject jump behind the verb.

sections.title: Everyday verbs used in this unit

blocks.text: Every Swedish verb has **one** present-tense form, and it ends in *-r*. That's the only feature you need to recognize for now; the verb groups are waiting in Unit 7.

**Att göra** is pronounced **aht YÖ-rah**, and its present form *gör* is pronounced **yör** — a *g* before *ö* sounds like *y*. The word turns up in one of the most frequent questions in Swedish: *Vad gör du?* ("what are you doing?"), pronounced **vah yör dü**.

blocks.title: Titta på, lyssna på
items: Swedish attaches **på** to some verbs of the senses: *titta **på** en film* (watch a movie), *lyssna **på** musik* (listen to music) — just like English "look **at**" and "listen **to**".
Dropping *på* changes the meaning: *titta* on its own just means "to look", with no object. Learn them as a pair: **titta på** and **lyssna på**.

exercises.prompt: Rewrite with the time or place expression at the front. Example: *Jag går hem idag.* → *Idag går jag hem.*
items: Vi åker buss till stan idag.
Hon jobbar på ett bibliotek på fredag.
De tittar på en film sedan.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Swedish. Watch where the verb goes.
items: In the morning the subway is always packed.

answers: På morgonen dricker jag kaffe. — Idag åker vi buss till stan. — På fredag jobbar hon på ett bibliotek. — Ikväll lagar jag mat. — Sedan tittar de på en film. — Imorgon är han ledig.
Idag går jag till universitetet. — På kvällen äter vi middag. — Varför sitter du här? — Jag förstår inte svenska. — Sedan tar hon tåget. — Imorgon jobbar jag hemma.
Idag jobbar jag hemma. — Ikväll tittar vi på en film. — På fredag är jag ledig. — Varför dricker du inte kaffe? — På morgonen är tunnelbanan alltid full.
